fragments.text: Methylene blue is a potent monoamine oxidase inhibitor: Methylene blue has been demonstrated to be a potent monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) and may cause potentially fatal serotonin toxicity (serotonin syndrome) when combined with serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs). (4) (see DRUG INTERACTIONS.) Serotonin toxicity is characterized by development of neuromuscular hyperactivity (tremor, clonus, myoclonus, and hyperreflexia, and, in the advanced stage, pyramidal rigidity); autonomic hyperactivity (diaphoresis, fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, and mydriasis); and altered mental status (agitation, excitement, and in the advanced stage, confusion). If methylene blue is judged to be indicated, SRIs must be ceased, prior to treatment/procedure/surgery.

fragments.text: Spontaneous reports of serotonin syndrome including fatal cases associated with the concomitant use of ZYVOX and serotonergic agents have been reported.

Commonly used serotonergic agents include serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants, buspirone, serotonin 5-HT1 receptor agonists (triptans), and opioids, including meperidine.

Monitor patients for the emergence of serotonin syndrome with the concomitant use of ZYVOX and serotonergic agents or with use of ZYVOX in patients with carcinoid syndrome. If signs or symptoms of serotonin syndrome occur, consider discontinuing ZYVOX and/or concomitant serotonergic agents as clinically appropriate and initiate supportive treatment.

mechanism: Additive serotonergic (pharmacodynamic) effect is the primary risk and is dose- and total-serotonergic-burden-dependent, so single-agent antitussive-dose dextromethorphan with an SSRI/SNRI carries low baseline risk. CYP2D6-inhibiting SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine) add a pharmacokinetic component by reducing dextromethorphan clearance and raising its exposure. This is additive PD risk, NOT an absolute contraindication (contrast the non-selective MAOI pairing, which is a separate contraindication rule: dextromethorphan__maoi_nonselective).

management.prescriber_action: Short-course single-agent dextromethorphan at the antitussive dose is usually acceptable alongside an established SSRI/SNRI. Risk of serotonin toxicity rises with high or misuse (recreational) dextromethorphan doses, with CYP2D6-inhibiting SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine) that raise dextromethorphan exposure, and when other serotonergic drugs are also present. Prefer a non-serotonergic antitussive if any of these apply or if the cough is not troublesome. Do not stop or alter the established SSRI/SNRI to accommodate an OTC cough remedy; refer to the prescriber if antitussive cover is genuinely needed in a higher-risk patient.
management.monitoring: Patient self-monitoring; no routine test. If dextromethorphan is used, watch for serotonergic features (agitation, tremor, myoclonus, sweating, fever) over the first day or two, especially at higher doses or with additional serotonergic drugs.
management.patient_counselling: Do not exceed the recommended antitussive dose and do not use dextromethorphan-containing products recreationally. Seek urgent help for agitation, confusion, tremor, muscle twitching or stiffness, sweating, fever, or a fast heartbeat. Keep taking your antidepressant as prescribed.
management.exceptions: Risk-dependent, not a flat contraindication: baseline risk with single-agent antitussive-dose dextromethorphan is low and rises with high/misuse dextromethorphan doses, CYP2D6-inhibiting SSRIs (fluoxetine, paroxetine), and additional serotonergic agents. Non-selective MAOIs are a separate, absolute contraindication (see dextromethorphan__maoi_nonselective).

If concomitant use of AUVELITY with other serotonergic drugs is clinically warranted, inform patients of the increased risk for serotonin syndrome and monitor for symptoms.

mechanism: Concomitant opioid and benzodiazepine or other CNS-depressant use may cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Gabapentinoid interactions are handled by the separate opioid__gabapentinoid rule.

management.prescriber_action: Reserve concomitant use for patients with inadequate alternative treatment options; prescribe the lowest effective doses and shortest duration of concomitant use. Do not stop opioid or benzodiazepine therapy that is established or specialist-directed without prescriber input.
management.monitoring: Monitor for profound sedation and respiratory depression, especially at initiation and after any dose increase of either drug.
management.patient_counselling: Warn about profound sedation, dizziness, and slowed or difficult breathing; avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants; ensure a carer or family member can recognise these signs and seek urgent help; consider take-home naloxone where appropriate.
management.duration: Shortest clinically appropriate duration of concomitant use.
management.exceptions: Established, clinically intended combinations require prescriber-led review and monitoring rather than unilateral interruption. The source explicitly addresses opioid use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants; the 22-member benzodiazepine-or-z-drug allowlist is the clinician-reviewable local mapping used by this rule.

mechanism: Gabapentin or pregabalin used with CNS depressants, including opioids, can cause serious respiratory depression; underlying respiratory impairment increases concern.

management.prescriber_action: Confirm that opioid plus gabapentin or pregabalin co-prescribing is intended. For a newly prescribed gabapentinoid, the prescriber should consider a low starting dose. Do not independently interrupt established opioid or gabapentinoid therapy.
management.monitoring: Monitor for respiratory depression and sedation, particularly with an opioid or underlying respiratory impairment.
management.patient_counselling: Sedation and breathing difficulty are the key risks; avoid alcohol and other sedatives; do not exceed prescribed doses; seek urgent help for excessive drowsiness, confusion, or slow/shallow breathing.
management.exceptions: This is not an absolute contraindication. Age, renal thresholds, high-opioid-dose claims, and third-agent modifiers are not encoded because the retained fragments do not establish them.

fragments.text: There is evidence from case reports, human studies, and animal studies associating gabapentin with serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression when coadministered with CNS depressants, including opioids, or in the setting of underlying respiratory impairment.

When the decision is made to co-prescribe gabapentin capsules with another CNS depressant, particularly an opioid, or to prescribe gabapentin capsules to patients with underlying respiratory impairment, monitor patients for symptoms of respiratory depression and sedation, and consider initiating gabapentin capsules at a low dose.

mechanism: The retained PARNATE evidence names pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, and ephedrine as contraindicated sympathomimetics with tranylcypromine because hypertensive reactions may occur. This rule is limited to those source-named decongestant members. Direct catecholamines are handled by the separate maoi_nonselective__direct_sympathomimetic diagnostic contraindication rule, with a monitored emergency-treatment exception. Tyramine is outside this drug-drug pack.

management.prescriber_action: Do NOT supply an OTC/indirect decongestant sympathomimetic (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, phenylephrine) to a patient on a non-selective MAOI. The MAOI is specialist-directed psychiatric therapy and must NOT be interrupted by the pharmacist: withhold the decongestant, clarify with the prescriber, and recommend a non-sympathomimetic alternative (e.g. saline nasal spray, nasal ipratropium, or a suitable antihistamine).
management.monitoring: If a dose has already been taken, monitor blood pressure and watch for hypertensive crisis (severe/throbbing headache, chest pain, palpitations, neck stiffness) and arrange urgent medical assessment.
management.patient_counselling: Avoid OTC decongestants and cold/flu combination products while on this medicine; always ask the pharmacist before buying any cold, flu, or sinus remedy. Seek urgent care for sudden severe headache, chest pain, or palpitations.
management.timing: Do not co-administer the covered decongestants during MAOI therapy. The retained fragment does not establish a post-discontinuation interval.
management.exceptions: Tyramine-rich foods are outside this drug-drug pack. Direct catecholamines are handled by maoi_nonselective__direct_sympathomimetic as a separate diagnostic contraindication with a monitored emergency-treatment exception. Neither rule is runtime-enabled.

mechanism: Additive serotonergic activity -> serotonin toxicity. This is the principal concern of the pair. It is NOT a reliable pharmacokinetic lithium-level interaction; SSRIs/SNRIs do not predictably shift lithium levels. Lithium-level change is driven by independent factors (renal function, sodium/fluid balance, intercurrent illness) handled by the separate lithium-monitoring rule, not by this serotonergic pair.

management.prescriber_action: Combination may be intentional (e.g. lithium augmentation of an antidepressant); use lowest effective doses and review total serotonergic burden. Do not stop established therapy unilaterally.
management.monitoring: Monitor for serotonin toxicity. Check a lithium level only when clinically indicated - renal impairment, sodium/fluid shifts, intercurrent illness, or a genuine pharmacokinetic interaction - not routinely, and not because an SSRI/SNRI was added.
management.patient_counselling: Report agitation, tremor, fever, sweating, or muscle twitching (serotonin toxicity). Separately, report lithium-toxicity signs (coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion) if dehydrated or unwell.
management.exceptions: The vague 'lithium level shift' rationale is removed: this pair is a serotonin-toxicity (additive PD) rule, kept at Moderate. Lithium-level monitoring is NOT strengthened here by renal impairment - renal-driven lithium accumulation is an INDEPENDENT lithium-monitoring rule evaluated on its own, so this serotonergic rule carries no renal context_modifiers.

fragments.text: Lithium can precipitate serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition. The risk is increased with concomitant use of other serotonergic drugs (including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, triptans, tricyclic antidepressants, fentanyl, tramadol, tryptophan, buspirone, and St. John's Wort) and with drugs that impair metabolism of serotonin, i.e., MAOIs [see Drug Interactions ( 7.1)].

Monitor all patients taking lithium for the emergence of serotonin syndrome. Discontinue treatment with lithium and any concomitant serotonergic agents immediately if the above symptoms occur, and initiate supportive symptomatic treatment.

_clinical_note: Newly-added SSRI/SNRI + lithium -> confirm_and_monitor (not counselling-only); principal concern serotonin toxicity. Lithium-level/renal accumulation is a SEPARATE independent lithium rule.

mechanism: Concomitant bupropion and antidepressant MAOI use increases hypertensive-reaction risk and is contraindicated.

management.prescriber_action: Do not co-prescribe bupropion with an antidepressant MAOI. Allow at least 14 days after stopping the MAOI before starting bupropion, and at least 14 days after stopping bupropion before starting an MAOI antidepressant.
management.monitoring: If exposure occurred, obtain urgent assessment for a hypertensive reaction.
management.patient_counselling: Seek urgent care for symptoms of a severe hypertensive reaction, such as a severe headache.
management.timing: Allow at least 14 days in both directions when switching between bupropion and an antidepressant MAOI.

mechanism: Additive CNS depression -> sedation and impaired psychomotor performance. Pharmacodynamic additive effect (not a contraindication).

management.prescriber_action: Prefer a non-sedating antihistamine where appropriate; avoid stacking sedatives. Consider dose/timing review in older adults or where falls, respiratory compromise, or occupational driving risk apply. This is additive pharmacodynamic sedation, not a contraindication - do not over-alert.
management.patient_counselling: Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how the combination affects you; avoid alcohol; expect additive drowsiness. Extra caution in older adults (falls/confusion risk).
management.exceptions: Systemic route only; topical/nasal/ophthalmic sedating antihistamines are out of scope. Do not unilaterally stop either an established antihistamine or an established CNS depressant - counsel and supply.
